22031-the-airplane-boys-among-the-clouds:
John Luther Langworthy's The Airplane Boys Among the Clouds came out in 1912, when flight was still new and dangerous. Its young heroes, the Bird boys, have spent the winter building a biplane in secret. Even their best friends were kept out of the colonel's workshop. The trial flight opens the book, and trouble follows at once.

A wreck, a rescue from the skies, and a mysterious Mr. Marsh keep the plot moving. The boys work with the local police chief against an unknown enemy. A race with a storm over Old Thunder Top caps the action. Such series books taught a generation of boys to dream in aeroplanes.
25762-billie-bradley-on-lighthouse-islan:
Janet D. Wheeler writes Billie Bradley on Lighthouse Island, or The Mystery of the Wreck, published by Cupples and Leon in 1920 with pictures. Wheeler, author of Billie Bradley and Her Inheritance and Billie Bradley at Three Towers Hall, fronts the book with girls reaching the point where the lighthouse stood.

Chapters open with lost, as a big drop splashes on Laura's nose, then a hut in the woods and ferns and mystery. Billie and her friends explore lighthouse island, chase a wreck's secret, and face storms and strangers, in a girls' series tale of courage, friendship, and detection.
44064-an-apology-for-the-life-of-mr-coll:
Colley Cibber told the tale of his own life on the London stage. A new form with notes by Robert Lowe came out in two books. This first book was one of a run of 510 fine copies. Parkes made twenty-six soft-ground portraits for it. Cibber calls his life tale an apology, in the old sense of a plea.

Actor, stage chief, and play maker, Cibber knew the boards well. He tells of plays, stars, and feuds of his long day. Lowe's notes and back parts fill gaps in the tale. Portraits of famed stage folk grace the pages. Stage past fans get a wit's own view of his age.
44065-an-apology-for-the-life-of-mr-coll:
Colley Cibber wrote an excuse for his own life in two books. Volume two is this copy of the player's famed tale. Five score times five plus ten copies were writ on fine leaf. That count is for England in this grand form of the work. The first book stands as its own text in the same set.

Stage wars, great names, and Cibber's own rise fill his tale. He tells of plays, kings, crowds, and his own sharp tongue at work. Each scene defends some act that foes had mocked in print. Wit and brass are his shield in all his long self plea. Stage past fans get a crown rogue's own brief. Few lives match its nerve.
53704-the-motor-boys-bound-for-home-or-n:
Clarence Young wrote The Motor Boys Bound for Home. Cupples and Leon issued it at New York in 1920. Ned, Bob, and Jerry ride on a wrecked troopship here. Twenty-one Motor Boys books line the front pages. The Jack Ranger series stands beside them. Turning Back opens this tale in chapter one.

Suspicions and The Little Man follow in turn. A Night Attack and A Midnight Blast build the sea peril. Disabled and The Mysterious Cabin come next. Whales crowd one lively picture plate. We are in the midst of a school of whales, Jerry shouts there. Boys home from the war meet wreck and riddle on the ocean road. A long-running boys' series sent its motor-mad trio through every machine age thrill the times could offer.
56400-memoirs-of-john-abernethy-with-a-v:
Memoirs of John Abernethy is a life of the great London surgeon, written by George Macilwain, one of his grateful pupils, and here in its third edition, printed in London in 1856. The title promises a view of Abernethy's lectures, writings, and character, with new extracts from original documents. A Shakespeare line on good and evil stands at the front.

Abernethy taught generations of surgeons at Saint Bartholomew's Hospital and was famed for his blunt, wise talk. Macilwain writes as a disciple, keen to fix his master's character before memory fades. The memoir gives his lectures' flavour, his views on medicine and surgery as one science, and the man himself. It is a warm record of a medical giant by a loyal student.
66201-the-life-and-works-of-joseph-wrigh:
William Bemrose wrote The Life and Works of Joseph Wright, the painter known as Wright of Derby, and Bemrose and Sons published it at London and Derby in 1885. Cosmo Monkhouse supplied a preface, and the book carries etchings and other plates. Wright had been a Royal Academician of high standing.

Bemrose says in his preface that Wright's name had sunk into half forgotten shade over the past fifty years, without good cause. An exhibition at Derby in 1883 had begun to restore his fame, and the book aims to carry that work further. It sets out the painter's life and discusses his pictures one by one. Art readers get a full case for a painter his home town still prized.
67526-letters-on-the-moral-and-religious:
Letters on the Moral and Religious State of South America was written by James Thomson and printed in London in 1827. Thomson wrote the letters while he lived for near seven years in Buenos Aires, Chile, Peru, and Colombia. He came home to England in 1825.

The letters were not first meant for print, and friends urged him to share parts of them. Thomson sorts the letters by place and theme for the book. He writes on faith, schools, morals, and daily life in the new states of South America. His aim, set out in the note to Lord Calthorpe, is the good of the people he lived among. The book gives an early British eye on lands just freed from Spain.
70588-richardson-s-new-london-fashionabl:
Richardson New London Fashionable Gentleman Valentine Writer is a love verse aid book. A Richardson house of Derby brought it out for the year use of beaux. Its next name calls it the lover own book for this year in full. A choice set of new and famed love day verses fills its scheme. Fit replies stand with each verse for the maid who gets one.

First comes a gent who weighs lone life gainst a wife and picks the wife. A young man near out of his trade time begs his maid to wait in verse. Yes and no replies both stand ready for that plea in rank. A house man would quit a fine post to serve his lass in verse. Trades, ranks, and moods shift through the set for each kind of beau.
britannica-1911-brynmawr:
Brynmawr is a market town of Brecknockshire, in Wales. It lies 156 miles from London by rail. Its urban district held 6833 people in 1901. This 1911 Britannica entry gives its railways and its past. A joint line links Rhymney and Abergavenny through the town. A branch runs to Pontypool. A Great Western line runs from Newport.

The town grew up around ironworks in the early 19th century. The works stood at the heads of valleys that meet nearby. The site was once called Waun Helygen, or Willow-tree Common. The Nantyglo ironworks employ many local people. The town's own coal is now exhausted. Its iron ore no longer suits modern processes. Brynmawr became a parish in 1875. It became an urban district in 1894. The district was enlarged in 1900.
